pdf_filename: An Investigation of the Influence of Learning Effectiveness and Motivations in a Taiwan History Digital Game – Govern Formosa.pdf

bibliographic.title: An Investigation of the Influence of Learning Effectiveness and Motivations in a Taiwan History Digital Game – Govern Formosa
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 26th International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2018)
bibliographic.publisher: Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education

study_characteristics.sample_description: Twenty-seven 5th grade students (13 boys and 14 girls) in a primary school in southern part of Taiwan
study_characteristics.aim: To investigate how the digital game Govern Formosa influences primary school students' learning effectiveness and motivations in history content about Taiwan in the late Qing dynasty

eligibility.concerns: No control group; small sample size (N=27); single class from one school

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes digital game-based learning as using educational digital games to integrate learning content (Taiwan history of late Qing dynasty) into gameplay. The game allows students to actively explore, observe, participate, and manipulate things in the digital game, learning through texts, graphics, and multimedia to retrieve relevant knowledge content. The game combines simulation, entertainment, and challenge with history content.

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Learning effectiveness measured via 20-item pretest/posttest (total score 100); Game questionnaire (24 items, 6-point Likert scale) measuring four aspects: motivation (5 items), system (5 items), content (5 items), and memory (9 items). Cronbach's alpha: pretest=0.843, posttest=0.963.
rq2.statistical_results: Learning effectiveness: pretest M=26.48 (SD=17.640) to posttest M=60.00 (SD=16.350), t=8.196***, p<.001. Motivation: pretest M=23.07 (SD=4.739) to posttest M=27.52 (SD=3.130), t=5.064***, p<.001. System: pretest M=24.41 (SD=3.703) to posttest M=26.81 (SD=4.161), t=3.314*, p=.003. Content: pretest M=24.63 (SD=3.477) to posttest M=27.37 (SD=3.564), t=3.635**, p=.001. Memory: pretest M=43.33 (SD=6.127) to posttest M=49.15 (SD=5.953), t=4.786***, p<.001.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Paired Samples t-test comparing pretest and posttest scores for learning effectiveness and all four questionnaire aspects (motivation, system, content, memory)
rq2.key_outcomes: All measures showed statistically significant improvements from pretest to posttest. Learning effectiveness scores more than doubled. Students' learning motivations significantly improved. The game was found to be feasible and effective for game-based learning in history courses. Students felt satisfied about the game and were willing to continue self-learning after school. A postponed test showed history knowledge memory was retained over time.
rq2.engagement_results: Students found the game intriguing and it attracted them to continue self-learning after school. Students were willing to play again. Memory aspect results showed students believed the game helped them memorize history content and connect to questions in assessments.

game_design_elements: Three progressive historical stages (Treaty Ports 1860s, SHEN Bao-Zhen 1874-1875, LIU Ming-Chuan 1885-1891)
Resource management (money, labor, crops: tea, sugar, camphor, rice)
3D scene exploration (Tamsui, Kaohsiung, Keelung, mountain area)
Task-based progression following real historical sequence
Strategy elements (choosing actions: trade, raise funds, reclamation, exploration)
2D map interface with color-coded administrative regions
Global map with country-specific crop trading values
technological_platforms: Google Maps reference for location scenes
instructional_strategies: Integration with formal 5th grade history curriculum (Ministry of Education Taiwan)
Historical content aligned with textbook and mid-term evaluation
Game used in conjunction with formal education history class
Two 40-minute sessions: 15 min pretest, 45 min gameplay, 15 min posttest, 5 min reflection
Content based on documentary books and historical references
rq3.content_integration: The game content is directly based on the primary schools history curriculum defined by Ministry of Education in Taiwan, covering Taiwan history in the late Qing dynasty. Three game stages correspond to three historical periods and events. Game events are ordered in real historical sequence. Learning assessment questions are adopted from history textbook, learning sheets, and mid-term evaluations. The 3D scenes are built based on history, documentary books, and Google Maps location references.

implementation_barriers: Need for more hints and information in the game to help students proceed
Need for more careful and detailed descriptions and clues as options
Balancing game play hours with lecture time ratio for effective learning
Game content must appropriately correspond to course content
methodology_limitations: No control group (single group pre-experimental design)
Single class from one school limits generalizability
Self-reported questionnaire for motivation and satisfaction
Experiment conducted before students had formal lessons on the topic
negative_effects: Students suggested the game needs more hints to give more information to proceed
System aspect showed smallest improvement among questionnaire dimensions
mitigation_strategies: Add a play-again button to allow students to revisit the game
Increase hints with more careful and detailed descriptions and clues
Implement more presentation modes in the game
Design game content to require more complicated thinking and reflections for deeper immersion
Future integration of three game stages into formal education courses separately
More qualitative analysis recommended to examine long-term vs short-term memory relationship

domain1.q1_evidence: The study focused specifically on 5th grade students studying Taiwan history in the late Qing dynasty, but inclusion/exclusion criteria for study selection are not detailed beyond the target population. One randomly selected class was used.
domain1.q2_evidence: Only 27 students from a single randomly selected class in one primary school in southern Taiwan participated. This is a convenience sample with very limited representativeness. No discussion of how this sample represents the broader population of 5th graders.

domain2.q3_evidence: The pretest/posttest items were adopted from history textbooks, learning sheets, and mid-term evaluations, reviewed and validated by history teachers. The questionnaire had good reliability with Cronbach's alpha of 0.843 (pretest) and 0.963 (posttest).
domain2.q4_evidence: Paired samples t-tests were used appropriately for pre-post comparisons. However, there is no reporting of effect sizes, no checking of normality assumptions with the small sample (N=27), and no correction for multiple comparisons across five separate t-tests.

domain3.q5_evidence: Results are generally interpreted consistently with the data. However, causal claims about the game's effectiveness are made without a control group, and the authors do not sufficiently acknowledge that the pre-post design cannot rule out alternative explanations (e.g., learning effects from simply engaging with the content, testing effects).
domain3.q6_evidence: The study does not include a formal limitations section. While recommendations for future research are mentioned (more qualitative analysis, integrating stages into formal courses), the fundamental methodological limitations (no control group, small sample, lack of generalizability) are not explicitly discussed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has significant methodological limitations: no control group (pre-experimental design), very small sample (N=27) from a single school, no formal discussion of limitations, multiple statistical tests without correction, and causal claims unsupported by the research design. While the measurement instruments show adequate reliability, the overall design provides weak evidence for the effectiveness claims made.
